## Source: amazon-inspector (b7192c53fc1e0b62e2c373a8a6beabfeb3777cae3aacfe23ca374eab1c2839a7)
The package impersonates the MLflow project (author 'MLflow Community' <community@mlflow.org>, homepage https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow) but provides no MLflow UI functionality. Both setup.py (install time) and mlflow_ui/__init__.py (import time) execute payload_core.py, which collects hostname, platform, the full process environment (dict(os.environ)), /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, /proc/self/cgroup, /proc/1/cmdline, directory listings of /, /app, /opt, /srv, /home, /tmp, and the output of `id`, `ps aux`, and `ip addr`, along with internal-network probe results. The data is base64-encoded and POSTed to https://webhook.site/9510ba0a-29f7-4ce6-afe7-632c92cf0f41/piprecon over TLS with verification disabled (ssl._create_unverified_context()). The same module fetches a second-stage Python payload from https://webhook.site/a9f5802b-c77e-4226-99dd-bc89d7dc8cca/s2.py and passes the bytes to compile()+exec() with subprocess and os bound in globals, yielding arbitrary remote code execution on the installer's host at both install and import time. Bulk environment scraping captures AWS_*, GH_TOKEN, npm/PyPI tokens, database URLs, and any other CI/build secrets present.

## Source: kam193 (efedaf471fdd5b95baee95d9bd0d330c8ce0f5da06b5cdf89458fd4ea7a38015)
During installation, the package first collects local information, environment variables, and probes connections to typically expected services like databanks. Results are exfiltrated and then, the next stage code is downloaded and executed. It then continues exfiltrating data by looking for credentials to databases, exfiltrating SQLite databases and bruteforcing&exfiltrating other databases reachable from the running environment.

## Source: amazon-inspector (0b3a5f6d1d39c20feca11d0129f0efa21bdf564586045555b756cc25bce73efc)
Package is advertised as a PDF converter but contains no PDF generation code. Its sole public method TXTtoPDFConverter.create_pdf(txt_path, pdf_path) is gated on the literal arguments 'file.txt' and 'file.pdf'; when matched, it invokes find_py_files() which walks the user's home directory, current working directory, and filesystem/drive roots via os.walk to collect up to 50.py source files, then _send_py_file() POSTs each file's bytes to https://api.telegram.org/bot<redacted>/sendDocument using a hardcoded bot token and chat_id 7481245219. A local sqlite database tracks already-exfiltrated files to avoid resending. Author metadata is placeholder ('YourName', 'A simple PDF converter library'), and the deceptive name targets developers searching PyPI for a PDF utility. Calling the advertised API silently routes the installer's source code to an attacker-controlled Telegram chat and produces none of the advertised functionality.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1 — CODE INTENT ANALYSIS:
Examine the code behavior in Section 1. What is the code actually doing?
Is this behavior consistent with the package's stated purpose, or is it
anomalous? Pay special attention to: setup.py hooks, __init__.py side-effects,
obfuscated strings, and network calls at import time.

STEP 2 — FALSE POSITIVE CHECK:
CRITICAL: Legitimate packages often use subprocess, exec(), socket, or
file I/O for standard build scripts, testing, or API features. If the
detected flow is clearly standard library functionality, well-documented
benign build tooling, or normal operations UNAMBIGUOUSLY consistent with
the package's stated purpose (e.g., an SSH library making SSH connections,
a cloud SDK reading cloud credentials) → mark as FALSE POSITIVE. However,
do NOT default to FALSE POSITIVE merely because the API usage pattern is
common or the package name sounds legitimate — a common API used for a
purpose UNRELATED to the package's stated function (e.g., unexpected
outbound network calls, credential access, or process execution with no
connection to any documented feature) remains a valid signal of malicious
intent, even if each individual API call looks unremarkable in isolation.
IMPORTANT — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT BY THEMSELVES EVIDENCE: patterns
such as "base64 decode + dynamic __import__/exec" or "extract a value from
incoming data + make an outbound request" are extremely common in
legitimate code (plugin/lazy-loading systems, compressed asset or config
decoding, webhook/event handlers, feature flags) and appear near-identically
across thousands of unrelated packages. A high similarity score to Section 2
built ONLY on this kind of generic shape — especially when the matched
neighbor itself has no specific attack-type tag or analyst description
confirming what it actually does — is weak evidence on its own. Weigh it
against the package's real, well-established purpose: for a package that is
one of the most widely used, foundational tools in its ecosystem (e.g. a
major testing framework, container/orchestration client, or database
driver), a single structurally-generic match is NOT sufficient grounds for
MALICIOUS — look for something SPECIFIC to this package's actual behavior
(concrete evidence of what the decoded/fetched content is used for, an
install-time hook, credential harvesting, etc.) before concluding malicious
intent for such a package.

STEP 3 — MALWARE SIMILARITY ASSESSMENT:
Compare with the known malware samples in Section 2. How structurally
similar is this code to known-malicious behavior? Consider: Are the data
flows (source → sink) analogous? Is the control flow pattern (gating
conditions) similar? Or is the similarity superficial (both use sockets,
but for entirely different purposes)? IMPORTANT: a high similarity score
(above ~0.90) to a matched sample remains meaningful evidence even when
that sample's own attack-type tag is "unclassified" — many confirmed
malicious samples in this dataset lack a specific label for data-sourcing
reasons unrelated to severity. Do not discount a strong structural match
solely because the matched neighbor's tag is generic.

STEP 4 — POLICY VIOLATION ANALYSIS:
Check each policy in Section 3. Does this code violate any of these
security policies? If so, which specific policy and why?

STEP 5 — MITRE ATT&CK MAPPING:
If the behavior appears malicious, map it to the most relevant MITRE
ATT&CK technique(s). Consider: T1059 (Command Execution), T1071
(Application Layer Protocol), T1005 (Data from Local System),
T1041 (Exfiltration Over C2), T1027 (Obfuscated Files), etc.

STEP 6 — SSVC RISK ASSESSMENT:
Apply the SSVC decision framework:
- Exploitation: Is this automatable? (yes/no)
- Technical Impact: partial or total?
- Decision: TRACK (benign/FP) | TRACK* (suspicious, monitor) | ATTEND (likely malicious) | ACT (confirmed malicious)
When the evidence is suggestive but not fully conclusive (e.g., moderate-
to-high similarity with plausible but not certain malicious intent),
prefer SUSPICIOUS/TRACK* over BENIGN/TRACK — flagging an ambiguous case
for review is preferable to silently missing a genuine threat. Reserve
BENIGN/TRACK for cases where the false-positive explanation from STEP 2
is clear and well-supported by the code's stated purpose.

reasoning.code_intent: The package overrides setuptools' `install.run` command hook to automatically execute arbitrary code upon installation. During installation, it gathers environment variables using `os.environ.copy()`, encodes payload data via `json.dumps` and `base64.b64encode`, and accesses system files.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: Collecting and base64-encoding environment variables during setuptools installation in a utility package named after a standard Python library function (`randrange`) is characteristic of supply chain credential theft and exfiltration.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Exhibits high structural similarity to known malicious packages that abuse installation hooks (e.g., `install.run`) to steal environment variables and exfiltrate sensitive data.

policy_violations.violation_reason: Employs data encoding routines (`base64.b64encode`) and dynamic execution within setup installation routines to obscure intent.

mitre_mapping.technique_name: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files or Environment Variables
mitre_mapping.relevance: Reads local environment variables (`os.environ.copy()`) during installation.
Executes malicious collection and encoding logic inside Python `setup.py` hooks.
Uses Base64 encoding to mask gathered environment and system data.

llm_evaluation.summary: The package `randrange` is malicious. It hijacks the `setuptools` installation process (`install.run`) to harvest environment variables (`os.environ.copy()`), serializes and encodes them using JSON and Base64, and exfiltrates system data upon installation. Immediate removal and credential revocation are strongly advised.

a cloud SDK reading cloud credentials) → mark as FALSE POSITIVE. However,
do NOT default to FALSE POSITIVE merely because the API usage pattern is
common or the package name sounds legitimate — a common API used for a
purpose UNRELATED to the package's stated function (e.g., unexpected
outbound network calls, credential access, or process execution with no
connection to any documented feature) remains a valid signal of malicious
intent, even if each individual API call looks unremarkable in isolation.
IMPORTANT — GENERIC CODE SHAPES ARE NOT BY THEMSELVES EVIDENCE: patterns
such as "base64 decode + dynamic __import__/exec" or "extract a value from
incoming data + make an outbound request" are extremely common in
legitimate code (plugin/lazy-loading systems, compressed asset or config
decoding, webhook/event handlers, feature flags) and appear near-identically
across thousands of unrelated packages. A high similarity score to Section 2
built ONLY on this kind of generic shape — especially when the matched
neighbor itself has no specific attack-type tag or analyst description
confirming what it actually does — is weak evidence on its own. Weigh it
against the package's real, well-established purpose: for a package that is
one of the most widely used, foundational tools in its ecosystem (e.g. a
major testing framework, container/orchestration client, or database
driver), a single structurally-generic match is NOT sufficient grounds for
MALICIOUS — look for something SPECIFIC to this package's actual behavior
(concrete evidence of what the decoded/fetched content is used for, an
install-time hook, credential harvesting, etc.) before concluding malicious
intent for such a package.

STEP 3 — MALWARE SIMILARITY ASSESSMENT:
Compare with the known malware samples in Section 2. How structurally
similar is this code to known-malicious behavior? Consider: Are the data
flows (source → sink) analogous? Is the control flow pattern (gating
conditions) similar? Or is the similarity superficial (both use sockets,
but for entirely different purposes)? IMPORTANT: a high similarity score
(above ~0.90) to a matched sample remains meaningful evidence even when
that sample's own attack-type tag is "unclassified" — many confirmed
malicious samples in this dataset lack a specific label for data-sourcing
reasons unrelated to severity. Do not discount a strong structural match
solely because the matched neighbor's tag is generic.
